prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Apart from its mass and width, the most important property of a new charged gauge boson, $W'$, is the helicity of its couplings to the SM fermions. Such particles are expected to exist in many extensions of the Standard Model. In this paper we explore the capability of the LHC to determine the $W'$ coupling helicity at low integrated luminosities in the $\ell +E_T^{miss}$ discovery channel. We find that measurements of the transverse mass distribution, reconstructed from this final state in the $W-W'$ interference region, provides the best determination of this quantity. To make such measurements requires integrated luminosities of $\sim 10(60) fb^{-1}$ assuming $M_{W'}=1.5(2.5)$ TeV and provided that the $W'$ couplings have Standard Model magnitude. This helicity determination can be further strengthened by the use of various discovery channel leptonic asymmetries, also measured in the same interference regime, but with higher integrated luminosities.

outputs.L1: Apart from its mass and width, the most important property of a new charged gauge boson, \(W'\), is the helicity of its couplings to Standard Model (SM) fermions. Such particles are predicted in many extensions of the Standard Model. In this paper, we investigate the LHC’s capability to determine the helicity of the \(W'\) couplings at low integrated luminosities using the \(\ell + E_T^{\mathrm{miss}}\) discovery channel. We find that the transverse-mass distribution reconstructed from this final state in the \(W\)–\(W'\) interference region provides the most effective determination of this property. Such measurements require integrated luminosities of approximately \(10\,(60)\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) for \(M_{W'}=1.5\,(2.5)\,\mathrm{TeV}\), assuming that the \(W'\) couplings have Standard Model magnitude. This helicity determination can be further strengthened through various leptonic asymmetries in the discovery channel, also measured in the same interference region, although higher integrated luminosities are required.
outputs.L2: Beyond its mass and width, a new charged gauge boson \(W'\) is characterized most crucially by the helicity structure of its interactions with Standard Model fermions. Bosons of this type are predicted by numerous extensions of the Standard Model. Here, we assess how effectively the LHC can identify the helicity of the \(W'\) couplings at relatively low integrated luminosity using the \(\ell+E_T^{\rm miss}\) discovery channel. Our results show that the strongest sensitivity comes from the transverse-mass spectrum reconstructed in the kinematic region where \(W\) and \(W'\) amplitudes interfere. Assuming couplings equal in strength to those of the Standard Model, this analysis requires approximately \(10~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) for \(M_{W'}=1.5~\mathrm{TeV}\) and \(60~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) for \(M_{W'}=2.5~\mathrm{TeV}\). Additional support for the helicity assignment can be obtained from several leptonic asymmetries in the same discovery channel and interference region, although these observables demand larger integrated luminosities.
outputs.L3:
The helicity structure of a new charged gauge boson’s couplings to Standard Model fermions is a fundamental property, comparable in importance to its mass and decay width. Many extensions of the Standard Model predict additional charged gauge bosons, commonly denoted \(W'\), whose interactions may be predominantly left- or right-handed. Determining this chiral structure is essential for identifying the underlying theory and distinguishing among different new-physics scenarios.

At the LHC, the coupling helicity of a \(W'\) can be investigated in the discovery channel \(W' \to \ell\nu\), which produces a charged lepton accompanied by missing transverse energy, \(\ell+E_T^{\mathrm{miss}}\). The key observable is the transverse-mass distribution, particularly in the kinematic region where the Standard Model \(W\) and the new \(W'\) amplitudes can interfere. Because the form and magnitude of this interference depend on the helicity of the \(W'\) couplings, the distribution below the \(W'\) mass peak provides information that is not available from the resonance signal alone.

Assuming couplings of Standard Model strength, a meaningful helicity determination would require an integrated luminosity of approximately \(10\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) for a \(W'\) mass of \(1.5\) TeV. For a heavier \(W'\) with a mass of \(2.5\) TeV, the lower production rate increases the required data sample to about \(60\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\). Leptonic asymmetries measured in the same \(W-W'\) interference region can provide additional sensitivity and strengthen the distinction between left- and right-handed couplings. Such asymmetry measurements are statistically more demanding, however, and therefore require larger integrated luminosities than an analysis based on the transverse-mass distribution alone.
outputs.L4:
This study investigates how the CERN Large Hadron Collider can determine the chiral—or helicity—structure of a newly discovered charged gauge boson \(W'\) using the standard \(\ell+E_T^{\rm miss}\) channel, where \(\ell=e,\mu\). The analysis considers a \(W'\) with Standard Model-strength couplings and compares the predictions for predominantly left- and right-handed interactions. Although the high-transverse-mass region provides the clearest discovery signal, events below the \(W'\) Jacobian peak are especially useful for diagnosing its couplings. In this region, a left-handed \(W'\) can interfere with the Standard Model \(W\) amplitude, whereas a right-handed state produces a characteristically different spectrum. The resulting distortions of the transverse-mass distribution therefore provide direct sensitivity to the helicity of the new boson.

The transverse mass,
\[
M_T=\sqrt{2p_T^\ell E_T^{\rm miss}\left(1-\cos\Delta\phi_{\ell\nu}\right)},
\]
is found to be the most powerful observable. Rather than relying only on the resonance region, the method exploits the shape and normalization of the distribution in the intermediate \(W\)–\(W'\) interference region. For a \(W'\) with Standard Model-like coupling strength, the left- and right-handed hypotheses can be distinguished with integrated luminosities of approximately \(10\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) for a mass of \(1.5\,\mathrm{TeV}\) and \(60\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) for a mass of \(2.5\,\mathrm{TeV}\). These results indicate that the chiral nature of a relatively light \(W'\) may be established with comparatively early LHC data, while heavier states require substantially larger event samples.

Leptonic asymmetries constructed from the charge and kinematic distributions of the observed lepton provide complementary information. Such observables retain sensitivity to the production dynamics and angular correlations associated with the \(W'\) couplings, but their statistical discrimination is generally weaker than that of the full transverse-mass spectrum at low luminosity. At higher luminosities, however, they can reinforce the helicity determination and offer an important consistency check. Overall, the analysis shows that the conventional discovery channel can do more than establish the existence and approximate mass of a charged resonance: by exploiting interference effects and differential distributions, it can also reveal whether the new gauge boson couples predominantly to left- or right-handed fermions.
outputs.L5:
### Apart, Such, Standard

Standing **apart** does not always mean being alone. Sometimes, it means refusing to accept a **standard** that no longer serves its purpose. **Such** choices may seem unusual at first, but they often lead to progress. Standards provide structure and consistency, yet individuality encourages creativity. The challenge is knowing when to follow established rules and when to step apart from them to create something better.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a particle physics paper investigating how the LHC can determine the helicity of a new charged gauge boson \(W'\) using the \(\ell+E_T^{miss}\) channel.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the sensitivity of the Large Hadron Collider to the chiral structure of a new charged gauge boson \(W'\) in the inclusive \(pp\to W'\to \ell\nu\) channel, characterized by a single energetic charged lepton and missing transverse momentum. Although the unobserved longitudinal momentum of the neutrino prevents full event reconstruction, information on the \(W'\) helicity couplings is retained in the lepton transverse-momentum and pseudorapidity distributions, the transverse mass, and charge-dependent observables. We show that interference between the Standard Model \(W\) amplitude and a left-handed \(W'\) provides an especially powerful discriminator from a right-handed state, including for resonance masses beyond the region with large on-shell event yields. After incorporating realistic acceptance requirements, detector effects, and dominant Standard Model backgrounds, we construct a likelihood analysis combining rate and shape information. We quantify the luminosity required to distinguish left- and right-handed coupling hypotheses as a function of the \(W'\) mass and width, and examine the impact of parton-distribution and normalization uncertainties. Our results demonstrate that the simple \(\ell+E_T^{\rm miss}\) final state can determine the chiral nature of a discovered charged resonance over a broad range of parameter space, complementing more exclusive decay channels and providing a direct probe of the gauge structure underlying the new interaction.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a collider phenomenology study of \(W'\) coupling helicity, emphasizing \(W\)–\(W'\) interference, transverse-mass distributions, leptonic asymmetries, and required integrated luminosities.
counterfactuals.output:
A \(W'\to \ell\nu\) search can probe not only the resonance mass and rate, but also whether the new charged current is left- or right-handed.

- **\(W\)–\(W'\) interference:** A left-handed \(W'\) couples to the same fermion helicities as the Standard Model \(W\), so the two amplitudes interfere. For the usual relative sign of the couplings, this interference is largely destructive between the \(W\) pole and the \(W'\) resonance. A purely right-handed \(W'\) does not appreciably interfere in the massless-fermion limit because it produces an orthogonal helicity state. The interference contribution can be sizable and should not be treated as a small correction to an incoherent signal-plus-background estimate.

- **Transverse-mass spectrum:** Because the neutrino longitudinal momentum is unknown, the principal observable is
  \[
  M_T=\sqrt{2p_T^\ell E_T^{\rm miss}\,[1-\cos\Delta\phi_{\ell\nu}]}.
  \]
  Both helicities produce a Jacobian edge near \(M_{W'}\), so the peak alone has limited chirality sensitivity. The key information lies in the broad region below the edge: a left-handed state produces an interference-induced deficit or distortion, whereas a right-handed state gives an approximately positive excess over the Standard Model spectrum. Fits should therefore include the full \(M_T\) shape and retain bins well below the resonance rather than imposing an excessively hard lower cut.

- **Leptonic asymmetries:** Charge-dependent lepton rapidity or pseudorapidity asymmetries, and reconstructed forward–backward-like asymmetries, provide complementary information. They exploit the proton PDFs to estimate the initial quark direction and the correlation between the charged lepton and the \(W'\) polarization. Such asymmetries are generally less powerful than the interference-driven \(M_T\) shape by themselves, but help resolve coupling mixtures, signs, and PDF/rate ambiguities.

- **Luminosity:** The requirement is strongly benchmark dependent. For an electroweak-strength \(W'\) in the roughly \(1\)–\(2\) TeV range at a high-energy LHC, discovery may require only a few to tens of \(\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\), while a statistically meaningful left-versus-right determination typically needs tens of \(\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\). Masses around \(2\)–\(3\) TeV or reduced couplings generally push the requirement toward \(100\ \mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) or several hundred \(\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\). Asymmetry measurements usually need more data than a simple spectral test.

The main conclusion is that helicity discrimination should be based on a combined likelihood using the full \(M_T\) distribution—including interference—and leptonic asymmetries. A resonance-only or narrow-window analysis can discover a \(W'\) while discarding much of the information needed to identify its chiral structure.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise research abstract explaining how to distinguish left- and right-handed \(W'\) couplings at the LHC for \(W'\) masses of 1.5 and 2.5 TeV.
counterfactuals.output: We study the discrimination of left- and right-handed \(W'\) couplings at the LHC in the process \(pp\to W'\to tb\), considering benchmark masses \(m_{W'}=1.5\) and \(2.5~\mathrm{TeV}\). The chiral structure is probed through top-quark polarization, measured using the charged-lepton helicity angle in semileptonic top decay, together with kinematic observables such as the reconstructed \(tb\) invariant mass and top transverse momentum. A left-handed \(W'\) also interferes with the Standard Model \(s\)-channel \(W\) amplitude, providing complementary sensitivity through rate and line-shape distortions, whereas a purely right-handed state does not. Template or likelihood fits to these observables, including detector acceptance, boosted-top reconstruction at \(2.5~\mathrm{TeV}\), and dominant background and systematic uncertainties, can therefore separate the two coupling hypotheses. The \(1.5~\mathrm{TeV}\) benchmark benefits from higher event yields, while the \(2.5~\mathrm{TeV}\) case relies more strongly on polarization-preserving boosted-object techniques.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the most effective observable for measuring the fermionic coupling helicity of a \(W'\) boson in its leptonic discovery channel, including quantitative luminosity estimates for Standard Model-strength couplings.
counterfactuals.output:
The most effective observable in \(W'\to \ell\nu\) is the **charged-lepton pseudorapidity charge asymmetry**
\[
A(\eta_\ell)=
\frac{d\sigma(\ell^+)/d\eta_\ell-d\sigma(\ell^-)/d\eta_\ell}
     {d\sigma(\ell^+)/d\eta_\ell+d\sigma(\ell^-)/d\eta_\ell}.
\]

Because the \(pp\) parton distributions preferentially boost the \(W'\) along the initial valence-quark direction, the \(V-A\) or \(V+A\) decay correlation becomes encoded in the shape of \(A(\eta_\ell)\). A left-handed \(W'\) and a right-handed \(W'\) therefore give characteristically different central-versus-forward asymmetries. This observable is preferable to a reconstructed rest-frame forward–backward asymmetry because it:

- uses only the measured lepton charge and pseudorapidity;
- avoids the twofold ambiguity in reconstructing the neutrino longitudinal momentum;
- cancels much of the luminosity, efficiency, and normalization uncertainty.

The transverse-mass spectrum below the Jacobian edge provides useful complementary information: a left-handed \(W'\) interferes with the SM \(W\), whereas a purely right-handed one generally does not. However, the lepton charge-asymmetry shape is usually the cleaner direct helicity discriminator.

For a \(14\)-TeV LHC and a sequential-\(W'\) normalization—fermionic couplings of approximately SM weak strength—typical parton-level/detector-level studies find that:

- \(\mathcal L\sim10~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) can distinguish left- from right-handed couplings for \(M_{W'}\) around \(1\!-\!2~\mathrm{TeV}\);
- \(\mathcal L\sim100~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}\) extends useful helicity discrimination to roughly \(M_{W'}\sim3~\mathrm{TeV}\).

Exact reaches vary with acceptance cuts, PDFs, backgrounds, and systematic errors, and the required luminosity scales approximately as \(1/g_{W'ff}^{\,2}\) when the event yield is the limiting factor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a technical paragraph on determining \(W'\) helicity at low LHC luminosity through the \(\ell+E_T^{miss}\) final state, comparing transverse-mass measurements with leptonic asymmetries in the interference region.
counterfactuals.output: At low LHC luminosity, the helicity—or, more precisely, the chiral fermion couplings—of a \(W'\) can be probed in \(pp\to W'\to \ell\nu\) using the \(\ell+E_T^{\rm miss}\) channel. The transverse mass, \(M_T=\sqrt{2p_T^\ell E_T^{\rm miss}(1-\cos\Delta\phi)}\), provides the most robust discovery and mass measurement through its Jacobian edge, but the high-\(M_T\) spectrum near the resonance is only weakly sensitive to left- versus right-handed couplings once rates and widths are adjusted. Greater discrimination can arise below the \(W'\) peak, where the Standard Model \(W\) amplitude interferes with a left-handed \(W'\) that couples to the same neutrino state, producing characteristic excesses or deficits, whereas a purely right-handed \(W'\) generally has negligible interference in the massless-fermion limit. Leptonic charge, rapidity, and reconstructed forward–backward asymmetries in this interference region retain information about the polarization-dependent decay angle and can therefore distinguish chiral hypotheses with fewer events than a resonance-shape fit. Their interpretation must nevertheless account for the unknown neutrino longitudinal momentum, the probabilistic assignment of the initial quark direction in a \(pp\) collider, parton-distribution uncertainties, and acceptance-induced asymmetries.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
